Life Dashboard/iPhone app

Apple Health, sent from your iPhone to your own server

Life Dashboard for iPhone is an open-source app (MIT license) that reads 28 Apple Health types and sends them to Home Assistant, an MQTT broker or your own webhook. It sends the same payload as the Android app, so both phones can share one server.

€6.99 once on the App Store, no subscription.

Build with Xcode

What it does

28 Apple Health types

Steps, sleep stages, heart rate, HRV, weight, blood pressure, glucose, VO2 max, workouts, nutrition and cycle tracking. Each starts off.

  • Every record, plus daily totals

    Each record names the app or device that wrote it. Daily totals count a walk recorded by iPhone and Watch once.

  • All your history

    Backfill from 30 days up to 5 years, or everything Apple Health has. A record you delete in Apple Health is reported to your server at the next sync.

  • Same payload as Android

    The Android app's keys, units and signing, so one Home Assistant or one receiver takes both phones.

  • Syncs in the background

    An interval or fixed times, with quiet hours. Most syncs come when you unlock the iPhone; a Shortcuts automation gives you an exact time.

  • Widget, Control Center, Siri

    See the last sync on your home screen, and sync from there, from Control Center on iOS 18, or with Siri.

Apple Health in Home Assistant, by QR code or over MQTT

The Life Dashboard integration pairs with one QR code and keeps every day in long-term statistics. Over MQTT, Home Assistant Discovery sets the sensors up without YAML, from the first sync on.

  • 20 of the 28 types as sensors Today's steps, distance and calories, and the latest heart rate, HRV, sleep, weight, blood pressure, glucose and VO2 max. The integration adds the last workout, sleep stages and what you ate today.
  • All your history With the integration, backfilled days land on their own date, as far back as Apple Health has data. Workouts and mindfulness count as hours per day.
  • Its own MQTT device and base topic lifedashboard-ios, so an iPhone never collides with an Android phone on the same broker.
Setup for the integration and MQTT

An Apple Health webhook with signed JSON

Any server that accepts a JSON POST can receive the data: n8n, Node-RED, the Grafana stack or a script. Every record carries a uuid to deduplicate on and a source that names the app or device that wrote it.

  • HMAC-SHA256 signing An optional X-Signature header, the same scheme as the Android app.
  • Client certificates (mTLS) Import a .p12 file into this iPhone's Keychain, for a server behind a reverse proxy that requires one.
  • A retry queue on the phone Every payload is queued before it's sent, so a sync that iOS cuts off loses nothing. It holds up to 700.
  • Every delivery on the Logs tab One row per delivery with its status, destination and time, a filter on failures, and the payload one tap further. Sync history folds out with deliveries, records and the latest failures.
The payload an iPhone sends

Runs in the background, within what iOS allows

HealthKit wakes the app for new data once the iPhone is unlocked, so most syncs come when you unlock it or open the app. A schedule is the earliest a sync may come, not a clock: an interval of an hour means at least an hour apart. For an exact minute, a Shortcuts automation runs Sync Health Data.

  • An interval or fixed times At least 15 minutes, 60 by default, on the weekdays you pick.
  • Quiet hours No sync between two times. Queued payloads wait too.
  • A locked iPhone can't be read iOS encrypts Apple Health while the iPhone is locked, so a sync waits until the iPhone is unlocked.
  • Shortcuts, widget and Control Center All three run Sync Health Data, together at most once a minute.

Life Dashboard for iPhone

Apple Health, with the same payload

€6.99 once (US$5.99), no subscription. No Mac needed, and it updates like any other app.

  • Build with Xcode AvailableFrom source, on a Mac with Xcode and an Apple Developer Program membership: about an hour the first time. Your settings stay when you run a newer version.

What you need

An iPhone on iOS 17 or newer. From the App Store, that's all: €6.99 once, no subscription. To build it yourself: a Mac with Xcode 26 (macOS 26.2 for the newest Xcode, or Xcode 26.3 on macOS 15.6) and an Apple Developer Program membership, because a free Apple Account can't sign an app that reads Apple Health; about an hour the first time, and the signature lasts a year. The Life Dashboard integration needs Home Assistant 2026.3 or newer, plus HACS on versions before 2026.11.

Sends to the Home Assistant integration, the Grafana stack, an MQTT broker or any webhook.

Questions about the iPhone app

What does building it take?

About an hour the first time, if you've never used Xcode. You need a Mac with Xcode 26 (the newest Xcode needs macOS 26.2; on macOS 15.6, Xcode 26.3 works) and an Apple Developer Program membership: Apple Health needs the HealthKit capability, which a free Apple Account can't sign. Then: 1. Clone the repository and open the project in Xcode. 2. Pick your own team for the app and the widget. 3. Give both your own bundle identifiers. 4. Replace the app group in three places (the two targets' capabilities and one line in SharedSyncStatus.swift). 5. Run it on your iPhone and allow Developer Mode once. The setup guide shows each screen. The signature lasts a year; run it from Xcode again to renew it.

Does it work with an Apple Watch?

Yes. The app reads what the Watch writes to Apple Health, and total calories arrive only on days with resting energy, which usually takes a Watch. HRV is SDNN, the measure Apple Health stores, so it isn't the same number as RMSSD from an Android watch.

Which languages is the app in?

Eleven: English, Dutch, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese (Brazil), Japanese, Arabic, Hindi and Simplified Chinese. It follows the iPhone's language, or the one you set for the app in Settings.

Does it send Screen Time?

No. Apple's Screen Time API shows usage only inside a report extension that runs in a sandbox with no network access, so no iOS app can send it anywhere. Screen time per app is in the Android app.

Can it write a scale reading into Apple Health?

No. The app asks Apple Health for read access only. Writing scale and blood pressure readings from Home Assistant into Health Connect is an Android feature.

How is it different from the Home Assistant companion app's Apple Health sensors?

Keep the companion app for presence and notifications. Its Apple Health sensors show today's total or the newest reading, and their history starts the day you switch them on. This app sends every record of 28 types, backfills all your history into Home Assistant, and also sends to MQTT or a webhook.

Can an iPhone and an Android phone share one Home Assistant?

Yes. Each phone gets its own device in the integration, and on MQTT the iPhone uses its own base topic. A settings backup moves between the two apps too. The same goes for your own webhook or MQTT broker: both apps send the same keys, units and signature, so one receiver takes both phones.

Can it send to Home Assistant and a webhook at the same time?

Yes. Every address has its own signing secret and headers, and pairing with Home Assistant sets them only for the address it adds, so a second receiver keeps its own. One thing to know today: a payload counts as delivered once one destination takes it, so a destination that's down at that moment misses it. The app can send to several webhooks and to MQTT at once.

Is it on the App Store?

Yes: Health Data for Home Assistant on the App Store, €6.99 once (US$5.99), with no subscription. It's the same app, built from the same MIT-licensed source, for people who'd rather not build it and want to support the project that way. Building it yourself costs nothing extra if you already have an Apple Developer Program membership: pull the repository and run it again to update; your settings stay. The releases on GitHub list what changed.

I don't have a Mac. Can I still use it?

Yes: install it from the App Store, which needs no Mac. Only building it yourself takes Xcode, which runs only on a Mac.

Can I build it with a free Apple Account?

No. An app that reads Apple Health needs the HealthKit capability, and only an Apple Developer Program membership can sign it; a free Apple Account can't. With a membership, building it yourself costs nothing extra and the signature lasts a year. Without one, the App Store version is the way.

Life Dashboard

Life Dashboard is an open-source project by Owen Vogelaar, in four parts: the Life Dashboard apps for Android and iPhone, a Home Assistant integration and a Grafana stack. It isn't related to other apps or templates called Life Dashboard. Questions go to Discussions.
